In control? Oh, I don't know about that. I don't really feel like I'm trying to control my life, necessarily. It's more just about keeping things safe. 

Although, speaking of being in control, my daughter Susan is certainly the one in control of her household. Goodness, she runs that place like a military operation! She has this enormous calendar on the wall in her kitchen, color-coded with all the children's activities. Soccer practice in blue, piano lessons in red... When she was a little girl, she took piano lessons from Mrs. Higgins down the street. Mrs. Higgins had this magnificent grand piano in her parlor, and a little white poodle named Fifi that used to sit under the bench and howl whenever Susan played a wrong note. It was the funniest thing! Susan hated practicing, though. She used to set the kitchen timer for exactly thirty minutes, and the second it dinged, she'd slam the piano lid shut and run outside to play hopscotch. We used to draw the hopscotch boards on the sidewalk with that thick, chunky chalk. Do they still make that chalk? The pink kind always seemed to break in half the minute you pressed down on it...

Oh, dear, listen to me. I've completely lost the thread again, haven't I? I am so sorry, doctor. You asked if checking makes me feel in control. No, I wouldn't say so. It just stops that awful nagging feeling that I've lost something important.

Well, no, it doesn't need to be perfect at all. I just need to know they are still there, safe and sound. I've never really been much of a perfectionist about how things look. 

Now, my old neighbor, Eleanor Gable, oh, she was a perfectionist. Her house was absolutely spotless. You could eat off the linoleum floor in her kitchen! And her rose garden... well, it was the envy of the entire neighborhood. She had these magnificent hybrid teas, the 'Peace' roses, you know the ones? Pale yellow with just a blush of pink at the edges. She used to spend hours out there with her little pruning shears, making sure every single bush was shaped just so. She'd wear this enormous straw hat with a green ribbon that tied under her chin to keep the sun off. One time, she pricked her finger on a thorn so badly it swelled up like a balloon, and her husband had to drive her all the way to the clinic in the next town over because our local doctor, Dr. Miller, was out fishing. Dr. Miller loved to fish down by the creek. He'd hang a little "Gone Fishing" sign on his practice door, just like in a cartoon! You simply can't imagine a doctor doing that nowadays, can you? He used to make house calls with a little black leather bag, and he always had butterscotch candies in his pocket for the children...

Oh, dear me. There I go again, talking your ear off about Dr. Miller's fishing trips. I am so sorry, I just get carried away. What were we saying? Oh, right, if things need to be perfect. No, no, the boxes and papers don't need to be perfectly organized or anything like that. I just need to lay eyes on them so I know they haven't been thrown out.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Uncomfortable when things aren't in their usual place? No, not really. I don't mind if things get moved around a bit. As long as I know they haven't been thrown away, I'm quite alright. 

My husband, Arthur, though, bless his heart, he was very particular about where things went. He had this wooden valet stand in the bedroom where he'd lay out his suit for the next day, right down to his cufflinks. He had the most beautiful pair of silver cufflinks with his initials engraved on them, a gift from his father when he graduated from university. Arthur studied engineering, you know. He always said a good engineer knows exactly where every tool in his box is. He had a workbench in the garage that was a marvel of organization. All those little glass baby food jars nailed by their lids to the underside of a shelf, sorted by the size of the screws and nails inside them. We must have fed our son David a hundred jars of strained peas just to get enough of those little glass jars. David hated the peas. He'd spit them right back out, and they'd get all over his little bibs. I used to soak those bibs in a bucket of water with a dash of bleach, out on the back porch...

Oh, good heavens, I'm doing it again. Talking about baby food jars and bleach. I apologize, doctor. My mind just wanders off down memory lane. You were asking about things being out of place. No, I don't need things to be in a specific spot. Just as long as they are still in the house and safe.

Harmful or contaminated? Oh, heavens no. No, I don't worry about germs or anything dangerous being in my things. They're just old papers and receipts, really.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Yes, I suppose it does make me feel more certain for a little while, but... well, honestly, that is exactly why I came to see you. I spend far too much of my day opening the exact same folders, the drawers, the labeled boxes, just over and over again. I have to make sure the important papers and keepsakes are exactly where I left them, even when I just checked them a few minutes before! It takes up my whole day. 

I keep a lot of the keepsakes in these sturdy boxes I bought years ago at Woolworths. Goodness, do you remember Woolworths? They had the absolute best lunch counter. I used to go there with my girlfriends when I was getting my degree, and we would sit on those spinning red vinyl stools and order cherry phosphates. My friend Beatrice always ordered a tuna melt, but she made them leave off the tomato because tomatoes gave her the most dreadful heartburn. And wouldn't you know it, she ended up marrying a man who ran a commercial tomato farm! Oh, the irony of it. They had a lovely outdoor wedding, but it rained pitchforks and hammer handles the entire afternoon. The canvas tent nearly blew right away into the neighbor's pasture, and the poor string quartet had to huddle under a tarp to keep their cellos from getting ruined...

Oh, my stars. I am doing it again. Rambling on about Beatrice and the rain. I am so sorry, doctor, I just lose my train of thought completely. But yes, checking makes me feel certain they are okay, it is just that I end up opening those same folders and drawers all day long to do it.

It's more just... I'd lose the history, you know? Well, I suppose it's the uncertainty. Not knowing is just an intolerable feeling. That's really why I came to see you in the first place, because the uncertainty makes me spend far, far too much of my day opening the same folders and drawers and labeled boxes again and again. Oh, dear. Listen to me, rambling on about green beans and train menus. I am so sorry, doctor. I don't know where my mind wanders off to half the time! Fear of making mistakes or feeling in control? You know, you asked me something very similar just a moment ago, and I'm still not entirely sure. I suppose... well, I don't really know if it's either of those things. It's just this feeling that things aren't right unless they're perfectly straight.

He would never let me drive if we were both in the car. We had this huge, heavy Oldsmobile Delta 88 back in the seventies. It was a sort of pale yellow color—'Harvest Gold,' they called it, which was everywhere back then. Our kitchen appliances were the exact same color! We had the refrigerator, the stove, even the toaster. Everything had to match. It was either Harvest Gold or that Avocado Green. My neighbor, Betty, had the green kitchen, and she had this terrible floral wallpaper to go with it... 

But Arthur loved that Oldsmobile. We drove it all the way down to Florida one winter to visit his brother in Boca Raton. It took us three days because Arthur refused to drive on the new interstate highways. He said they were too impersonal and you couldn't see the real America. So we took all these little two-lane roads through the Carolinas and Georgia. We stopped at this roadside stand in Georgia that sold boiled peanuts. I had never had a boiled peanut in my life! They were so soft and salty, completely different from the roasted kind you get at a baseball game. We used to go to Ebbets Field to see the Dodgers before they moved to California. My father would take me, and we'd sit in the bleachers...

Oh, dear. Boiled peanuts and the Brooklyn Dodgers. I've done it again, haven't I? I am so sorry, doctor. My mind just takes a thought and runs right out the door with it. But truly, I don't know if it's about control or mistakes. I just know the edges have to be perfectly straight, or I can't rest.
